notes.crossReferenceNotes: Daniel 5:30-31 records Babylon's fall. Daniel 6:1 introduces Darius' administration.

symbols.symbol: Literary image: first year of Darius
symbols.meaning: Daniel 9 opens in the first year of Darius, the son of Ahasuerus, of the seed of the Medes, about 539/538 B.C. It functions here as a narrative image or motif rather than a separate coded prophecy.

wordNotes.explanation: Daniel 9 opens in the first year of Darius, the son of Ahasuerus, of the seed of the Medes, about 539/538 B.C.
Daniel 9 opens in the first year of Darius, the son of Ahasuerus, of the seed of the Medes, about 539/538 B.C.

notes.crossReferenceNotes: Daniel reads Jeremiah's seventy years before Gabriel gives the seventy weeks, so Scripture study becomes the doorway to prayer and further light.

symbols.meaning: The written promise that moves Daniel from prophetic study into confession and intercession.

wordNotes.explanation: Daniel understands by the books the number of years spoken by Jeremiah: Jerusalem's desolations would last seventy years.
Jeremiah had said that Judah would serve Babylon seventy years and that God would visit His people afterward.

notes.crossReferenceNotes: Daniel responds to prophecy with humility rather than speculation.

symbols.meaning: Visible signs of grief, humility, and repentance before God.

wordNotes.explanation: Daniel sets his face unto the Lord God, seeking by prayer, supplications, fasting, sackcloth, and ashes.
Fasting, sackcloth, and ashes belong to repentance and mourning.

notes.crossReferenceNotes: Daniel appeals to God's covenant character before confessing the people's covenant failure.

symbols.meaning: God's faithful love as the basis for confession, obedience, and restoration.

wordNotes.explanation: God keeps covenant and mercy; the people have broken covenant and need mercy.
Daniel begins by confessing and by naming God as great, dreadful, covenant-keeping, and merciful toward those who love Him and keep His commandments.

notes.crossReferenceNotes: Psalm 51 models personal confession. Leviticus 26:40-42 promises that if Israel confesses iniquity, God will remember His covenant.

symbols.meaning: Daniel confesses, 'We have sinned.' He includes perversity, wickedness, rebellion, and departure from God's precepts and judgments. It functions here as a narrative image or motif rather than a separate coded prophecy.

wordNotes.explanation: Daniel confesses, 'We have sinned.' He includes perversity, wickedness, rebellion, and departure from God's precepts and judgments.
The prayer does not soften sin or excuse the people by blaming Babylon.

notes.crossReferenceNotes: Jeremiah 7:25-26 God sent His servants the prophets, but the people did not listen. 2 Chronicles 36:15-16 Judah mocked God's messengers until there was no remedy.

symbols.symbol: Literary image: people of the land
symbols.meaning: Daniel confesses that the people have not listened to the prophets who spoke in God's name to kings, princes, fathers, and all the people of the land. It functions here as a narrative image or motif rather than a separate coded prophecy.

wordNotes.explanation: Daniel confesses that the people have not listened to the prophets who spoke in God's name to kings, princes, fathers, and all the people of the land.
Kings were warned, leaders were warned, ancestors were warned, and ordinary people were warned.

notes.crossReferenceNotes: 1 Kings 8:46-49 anticipates Israel scattered far and near, praying toward the land. Isaiah 57:19 speaks peace to those far and near.

symbols.meaning: Daniel declares that righteousness belongs to the Lord, but confusion of faces belongs to Judah, Jerusalem, all Israel, near and far, because of their trespass. It functions here as a narrative image or motif rather than a separate coded prophecy.

wordNotes.explanation: Daniel declares that righteousness belongs to the Lord, but confusion of faces belongs to Judah, Jerusalem, all Israel, near and far, because of their trespass.
Daniel mentions those near and far because covenant mercy must reach exiles wherever judgment has driven them.

notes.crossReferenceNotes: 2 Chronicles 36:14 priests and people transgressed greatly. Jeremiah 44:21 names fathers, kings, princes, and people in covenant guilt.

symbols.meaning: Daniel repeats that confusion of face belongs to kings, princes, fathers, and the people because they have sinned against God. It functions here as a narrative image or motif rather than a separate coded prophecy.

wordNotes.explanation: Daniel repeats that confusion of face belongs to kings, princes, fathers, and the people because they have sinned against God.
Leaders are named again because their responsibility was real.

notes.crossReferenceNotes: Psalm 86:5 God is good, ready to forgive, and abundant in mercy. 1 John 1:9 promises forgiveness and cleansing when sins are confessed.

symbols.meaning: After confessing shame, Daniel turns to mercy: 'To the Lord our God belong mercies and forgivenesses, though we have rebelled against him.' The hope of the prayer rests entirely in God's character. It functions here as a narrative image or motif rather than a separate coded prophecy.

wordNotes.explanation: After confessing shame, Daniel turns to mercy: 'To the Lord our God belong mercies and forgivenesses, though we have rebelled against him.' The hope of the prayer rests entirely in God's character.
Mercy and forgiveness are plural in the KJV, giving the sense of abundant compassion.

notes.crossReferenceNotes: Deuteronomy 6:4-6 links hearing God with loving and obeying Him. Psalm 119 celebrates walking in God's law.

symbols.symbol: Literary image: voice of the LORD
symbols.meaning: Daniel confesses that the people have not obeyed the voice of the Lord by walking in His laws, which He set before them through the prophets. It functions here as a narrative image or motif rather than a separate coded prophecy.

wordNotes.explanation: Daniel confesses that the people have not obeyed the voice of the Lord by walking in His laws, which He set before them through the prophets.
Sin is described as refusal to walk in revealed light.

notes.crossReferenceNotes: Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28-30 set out covenant blessings, curses, exile, confession, and restoration. 2 Chronicles 36:21 exile with the land's Sabbath rest.

symbols.meaning: Therefore the curse written in the law of Moses has been poured upon them. It functions here as a narrative image or motif rather than a separate coded prophecy.

wordNotes.explanation: Therefore the curse written in the law of Moses has been poured upon them.
Therefore the curse written in the law of Moses has been poured upon them.

notes.crossReferenceNotes: 2 Kings 24-25 and 2 Chronicles 36 describe Jerusalem's destruction. Lamentations mourns the disaster.

symbols.symbol: Literary image: under the whole heaven
symbols.meaning: Daniel says there had not been such evil under the whole heaven as what came upon Jerusalem. It functions here as a narrative image or motif rather than a separate coded prophecy.

wordNotes.explanation: Daniel says there had not been such evil under the whole heaven as what came upon Jerusalem.
Daniel acknowledges that God has confirmed His words against the people and judges, bringing a great evil upon Jerusalem.

notes.crossReferenceNotes: Daniel 12:10; Hosea 6:1-3; Jeremiah 29:12-14; John 7:17.

symbols.meaning: Daniel says the evil came as written in the law of Moses, yet the people did not make their prayer before the Lord, turn from iniquities, or understand His truth. It functions here as a narrative image or motif rather than a separate coded prophecy.

wordNotes.explanation: Daniel says the evil came as written in the law of Moses, yet the people did not make their prayer before the Lord, turn from iniquities, or understand His truth.
Daniel says the evil came as written in the law of Moses, yet the people did not make their prayer before the Lord, turn from iniquities, or understand His truth.

notes.crossReferenceNotes: Deuteronomy 28; Jeremiah 1:12, where God watches over His word to perform it; Daniel 7:9-10, where the heavenly court opens the books.

symbols.symbol: Literary image: watched upon the evil
symbols.meaning: Daniel says the Lord watched upon the evil and brought it upon them, for He is righteous in all His works, yet the people did not obey His voice. It functions here as a narrative image or motif rather than a separate coded prophecy.

wordNotes.explanation: Daniel says the Lord watched upon the evil and brought it upon them, for He is righteous in all His works, yet the people did not obey His voice.
He says God is righteous.

notes.crossReferenceNotes: Exodus 12-15; Deuteronomy 26:5-8; Joshua 2:9-10; Psalm 77:13-15.

symbols.symbol: Literary image: brought thy people forth out of the land of Egypt
symbols.meaning: Daniel now appeals to the God who brought His people out of Egypt with a mighty hand and made Himself a name. It functions here as a narrative image or motif rather than a separate coded prophecy.

wordNotes.term: brought thy people forth out of the land of Egypt
wordNotes.explanation: Daniel now appeals to the God who brought His people out of Egypt with a mighty hand and made Himself a name.
Both deliverances depend on God's name and mighty hand.

notes.crossReferenceNotes: 1 Kings 8:29-30; Psalm 48; Psalm 79; Isaiah 2:2-4.

symbols.symbol: Literary image: fury be turned away
symbols.meaning: Daniel pleads that according to all God's righteousness, His anger and fury be turned away from Jerusalem, His holy mountain. It functions here as a narrative image or motif rather than a separate coded prophecy.

wordNotes.explanation: Daniel pleads that according to all God's righteousness, His anger and fury be turned away from Jerusalem, His holy mountain.
The holy mountain language points to Jerusalem as more than a city on a map.

notes.crossReferenceNotes: Daniel's prayer about the desolate sanctuary belongs beside Daniel 8's promise that the sanctuary will be cleansed or restored.

symbols.meaning: The ruined earthly sanctuary that burdens Daniel and connects his prayer with the sanctuary vision of Daniel 8.

wordNotes.explanation: Daniel asks God to hear his prayer and supplications and to cause His face to shine upon His desolate sanctuary, for the Lord's sake.
The request for God's face to shine echoes priestly blessing and covenant favor.

notes.crossReferenceNotes: Psalm 51:1; Isaiah 64:6; Romans 3:21-26; Titus 3:5.

symbols.meaning: He does not present Israel's righteousness as the basis of the plea, but God's great mercies. It functions here as a narrative image or motif rather than a separate coded prophecy.

wordNotes.explanation: He does not present Israel's righteousness as the basis of the plea, but God's great mercies.
Daniel asks God to incline His ear and open His eyes to the desolations and to the city called by His name.

notes.crossReferenceNotes: 1 Kings 8:30; Psalm 79:9; Zechariah 1:12; Daniel 9:23.

symbols.meaning: He asks for action not for the people's sake alone, but for God's own sake. It functions here as a narrative image or motif rather than a separate coded prophecy.

wordNotes.explanation: He asks for action not for the people's sake alone, but for God's own sake.
The city and people are called by His name.

notes.crossReferenceNotes: Isaiah 65:24 God answers before His people finish speaking. Daniel 6:10 shows Daniel's lifelong prayer habit.

symbols.meaning: While Daniel is speaking, praying, confessing his sin and the sin of his people Israel, and presenting supplication for God's holy mountain, heaven is already moving. It functions here as a narrative image or motif rather than a separate coded prophecy.

wordNotes.explanation: While Daniel is speaking, praying, confessing his sin and the sin of his people Israel, and presenting supplication for God's holy mountain, heaven is already moving.
He knows his own need, his people's guilt, and God's holy mountain.

notes.crossReferenceNotes: Gabriel's return links Daniel 9 to Daniel 8, and the evening offering keeps the sanctuary burden in view.

symbols.meaning: Sanctuary time remembered even while the earthly temple is desolate.

wordNotes.explanation: Gabriel, the man Daniel had seen in the earlier vision, comes swiftly and touches him about the time of the evening oblation.
The reference to the earlier vision points back to Daniel 8, where Gabriel was commanded to make Daniel understand.

notes.crossReferenceNotes: Daniel 8:16-17; Daniel 8:26-27; Daniel 10:12-14.

symbols.meaning: Gabriel says he has come to give Daniel skill and understanding. It functions here as a narrative image or motif rather than a separate coded prophecy.

wordNotes.explanation: Gabriel says he has come to give Daniel skill and understanding.
This echoes the command in Daniel 8:16, where Gabriel was told to make Daniel understand the vision.

notes.crossReferenceNotes: Daniel 9 continues the explanation of Daniel 8 by addressing the unresolved time prophecy through the seventy weeks.

symbols.meaning: Gabriel points Daniel back to the unresolved vision of Daniel 8, especially the time element.

wordNotes.explanation: Then he tells him to understand the matter and consider the vision.
Gabriel says the commandment came forth at the beginning of Daniel's supplication because Daniel is greatly beloved.

notes.crossReferenceNotes: The seventy weeks are marked off for Israel and Jerusalem, but their redemptive goals center in Messiah and connect to the sanctuary prophecy.

symbols.meaning: Four hundred ninety prophetic years marked off for Daniel's people and city, opening the larger 2300-year period.
Sanctuary language pointing to the consecration and fulfillment connected with Messiah's work.

wordNotes.explanation: Gabriel begins with a measured period: seventy weeks are determined upon Daniel's people and the holy city.
God will finish transgression, make an end of sins, make reconciliation for iniquity, bring in everlasting righteousness, seal up vision and prophecy, and anoint the Most Holy.

notes.crossReferenceNotes: The decree of Artaxerxes in 457 B.C. begins the count that reaches to Christ's baptism and anointing in A.D. 27.

symbols.meaning: The restoration decree that best fits the command to restore and build Jerusalem.
Jesus publicly anointed at His baptism in A.D. 27 at the end of sixty-nine prophetic weeks.

wordNotes.term: commandment to restore and to build Jerusalem
wordNotes.explanation: Gabriel gives the starting point: from the commandment to restore and build Jerusalem until Messiah the Prince are seven weeks and sixty-two weeks.
That is the year Jesus was baptized and anointed by the Holy Spirit, beginning His public ministry as Messiah.

notes.crossReferenceNotes: Messiah's death belongs inside the seventy-week flow, while the later destruction of Jerusalem follows as a solemn consequence.

symbols.meaning: Christ's sacrificial death after the sixty-nine weeks, not for Himself but for sinners.

wordNotes.explanation: After the sixty-two weeks, Messiah is cut off, but not for Himself.
The line then looks beyond the cross to the destruction of the city and sanctuary by the people of the prince that shall come.

notes.crossReferenceNotes: Daniel 9:27 points to Christ confirming the covenant and fulfilling sacrifice, not to a postponed future seven-year tribulation week.

symbols.meaning: Christ confirming God's covenant through His ministry, death, and the apostolic witness to Israel.
The sacrificial system fulfilled by Christ's once-for-all offering in the midst of the seventieth week.

wordNotes.explanation: He confirms the covenant with many for one week, and in the midst of the week He causes sacrifice and oblation to cease.

wordNotes.term: sacrifice and the oblation to cease
wordNotes.explanation: Jesus does not abolish sacrifice by desecrating a temple; He fulfills sacrifice by offering Himself once for all.
